name: OAuth2 provider selector
purpose: The optional sign-in UX for projects configured with more than one provider. Renders a list of the configured providers by their operator-visible `label` and routes each choice to `/auth/sign-in?provider=<id>`. Optional at wire time: a project may substitute a bespoke selector surface as long as it honours the query-parameter contract on the sign-in route.
responsibilities: Read the provider-config list at request time and render one item per provider record whose `enabled` field is true (or absent, defaulting to enabled) (AC-10109-1).

Render each item as a link (or a form-post button, per the wiring shim's declared class) whose target is `/auth/sign-in?provider=<id>`; render the item's operator-visible `label` as the visible text (AC-10109-1).
Short-circuit when N==1: a request to the selector route with a single-provider configuration returns a 302 to `/auth/sign-in?provider=<the-single-id>` instead of rendering a list (REQ-009).

Refuse to render on an empty provider-config list with a stable-coded error page code `OAUTH2_NO_PROVIDERS_CONFIGURED`; this is a boot-time refusal in the reference wiring, not a run-time page (REQ-009).
internalStructure: One factory function producing a request-handler closure over an injected `providerConfig` module. The reference wiring is framework-agnostic and returns a plain HTML string; framework shims (an Express handler, a Fastify handler, a Workers fetch wrapper) are one-file adapters colocated with this TAC's module directory. A project that wants a React or Vue rendering substitutes its own selector surface that hits the same query-parameter contract.

interfaces.name: providerConfig
interfaces.description: The provider-config module (same source as TAC-1102 reads); exposes `list() -> record[]` and the enabled flag.

dependencies.name: OAuth2 provider adapter
dependencies.description: Reads the same provider-config the adapter validates at boot.

tradeoffs: A first-party selector surface makes the multi-provider posture visible without a project-side page implementation; the cost is one rendering path the blueprint owns and a small piece of style the project may want to override. Substituting a bespoke selector is a plain wire swap on the sign-in route; the query-parameter contract is the seam, not the rendering. Not owning the sign-in initiation logic (that belongs to the flow controller) keeps this TAC's surface small: it is a route that renders a list and links; the state machine is elsewhere.
